newsitem.title: USA: Price fears may spark spring Fed rate hike - experts.
newsitem.headline: Price fears may spark spring Fed rate hike - experts.

text.p: U.S. inflation remains subdued but the Federal Reserve could tighten monetary policy as soon as May in a pre-emptive move to prevent the slumbering giant from awakening, Wall Street analysts said.
Experts said tight labor markets and recent jitters about the future performance of the U.S. dollar have raised a yellow flag and left policy makers wary of possible upward inflationary pressures.

"I've long thought Fed (policy makers) will be patient and they will tighten monetary policy when they have persuasive evidence that inflation risks are rising," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank.
"We haven't seen that yet. But I think we will see it by the spring and therefore I would look to the May meeting as the most likely date at which they would engineer a tightening," he added.
Although the January employment data released last Friday was widely regarded as a benign report, some analysts said it bore a few worrisome signs.
The pundits said a 271,000 rise in non-farm payrolls in January against a 261,000 increase in the previous month was by itself very strong and well north of most forecasts.
"As long as the economy is operating at these high levels of employment ... inflation remains a risk," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.

Thus, those analysts said a slight drop in the average weekly hours to 34.1 in January from 34.8 earlier was mostly weather-related, adding that the indicator should come back up in the next few months.

"We, at least on the employment report, are reading the evidence differently. There's very strong momentum in these wage numbers that we think is worrisome," said David Hensley, an economist at Salomon Brothers.

"Our sense is that the Fed would intervene and take out some insurance against a possible accelaration in overall price inflation ... We think that we're looking at that situation by spring, certainly by mid-year," Hensley added.
Fed Board members usually keep a close eye on employment data because possible higher income might fuel demand and drive up inflationary pressures as a result.
"The employment report bolsters the case for a Fed tightening down the road," said Christopher Rupkey, vice president at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
"The economy is running along fast enough that eventually the Fed will tighten by mid-year," he added.

Uncertainty about the performance of the U.S. dollar against other major currencies was seen as another reason why the Federal Reserve might notch up interest rates as a pre-emptive strike against inflation.
The market's dollar concerns were triggered by remarks late last week by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin who said the dollar has been stong "for some time."

Following Rubin's remarks, the Group of Seven industrialized nations (G-7) signaled unity in their desire to arrest the dollar's recent rise against major foreign currencies. G-7 officials met last Saturday in Berlin.
Most Wall Street economists agree the dollar's rapid ascent -- mainly against the yen and the mark -- has been a factor in keeping inflation low by capping imported goods' prices.
Prospects for a stable or even lower dollar in the coming months could minimize or maybe wipe out the foreign exchange factor in controlling inflation, analysts said.

In an effort to gauge the impact of a strong dollar in the domestic economy, economists said the rule of thumb is that a 10 percent appreciation of the dollar might, in a three-year time horizon, chop as much as one percentage point off of the overall Consumer Price Index (CPI).

The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta trade-weighted dollar index of 18 major currencies showed the greenback rose an overall 9.94 percent in the period between April 1995, when the dollar bottomed out after a steep drop, and January 1997.
The rise was seen as significant in helping to keep inflation under control even though the currency rose much less or even fell when some key currencies are factored out of the index.
However, the lag between factors such as wage increases and a stable or slightly weaker dollar and inflation led analysts to say they expected no inflation boom in 1997.
"The core (CPI) rate might go up a bit, but the overall rate might come back down because energy prices have moderated," Bank of Tokyo's Rupkey said.

On average, analysts expect the CPI to remain unchanged or rise slightly this year to between 3.0 and 3.3 percent. The core rate, which excludes food and energy price fluctuations, is seen rising to around 3.0 percent from 2.6 percent in 1996.
The Fed last changed monetary policy in January 1996, when it trimmed its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.25 percent.
